title: Design a URL Shortener
subtitle: The hello world of system design — and it's deeper than it looks
objectives: Turn a vague prompt into requirements and back-of-envelope numbers
Design the key generation scheme, and defend it against the obvious alternatives
Apply the read-heavy playbook: caching, replicas, and where the truth lives
Handle the real edges: collisions, custom aliases, expiry, and analytics at scale

exercises.title: A design prompt is deliberately under-specified — your first move is to make it specific
exercises.body: 'Design a URL shortener' is not a spec, it's an invitation to guess. Before you name a database, extract four things: what it must do, how many writes, how many reads, and the ratio between them. A shortener at 100 links a day and one at 100 million share a name and nothing else. The arithmetic tells you which of your problems are real.
exercises.note: Estimation isn't a warm-up ritual — it's how you find out which problems are imaginary. Most of what gets over-built here is defence against a bottleneck the numbers would have ruled out in thirty seconds.

exercises.prompt: 'Design a URL shortener.' What's the first move?
choices: Pin down requirements and scale: what must it do, how many writes, how many reads, and what's the read:write ratio
exercises.why: Every later decision is downstream of those numbers — a shortener at 100 links a day and one at 100 million are different systems, and you can't defend a cache or a shard without knowing the shape of the load. The read:write ratio in particular decides almost everything here, which is why it's worth extracting before you name a single technology.

exercises.prompt: Which are the core functional requirements? Select all.
choices: Given a long URL, return a short one
Given a short URL, redirect to the long one
exercises.why: Shorten, redirect, and optionally expire — that's the product. Collaborative editing is invented scope, and noticing what's NOT required is as valuable as listing what is: every requirement you accept has to be defended in the design, so smuggling in extras costs you real complexity for imaginary users.

exercises.prompt: 100 million new links per day. Roughly how many writes per second on average?
exercises.why: There are ~86,400 seconds in a day, so 100M ÷ 86,400 ≈ 1,160/sec. That's a modest number — well within one well-tuned database — which is the first genuinely useful finding: the write path is not where the difficulty lives, and peaks will run several times the average, so size for maybe 3–5× this.

exercises.prompt: Reads are 100× writes. So ~116,000 redirects/second. What does that ratio tell you about the design?
choices: It's overwhelmingly a read system — so caching and replicas carry the design, and the write path can stay simple
exercises.why: A 100:1 ratio means the redirect is the product and everything else is bookkeeping, so your effort belongs in serving reads cheaply — cache, replicas, and a CDN-friendly redirect. It also means unit 7's rule applies directly: put the work where the traffic isn't, and the traffic is reads.

exercises.prompt: Each link record is roughly 500 bytes. Storing 100 million links per day for 5 years — roughly how many terabytes?
exercises.why: 100M × 500 bytes = 50GB/day; × 365 × 5 ≈ 91TB. Big enough that one machine's disk is a real question, small enough that it isn't frightening — which is exactly the kind of finding that decides whether unit 15's sharding is on the table or premature.

exercises.prompt: Your estimates say ~1,200 writes/sec and ~91TB over five years. What have you learned?
choices: You need a massive distributed system
Writes are easy and storage is the growth problem — so the design questions are the read path and how the data is partitioned over time, not write throughput
You need to shard by user
exercises.why: The arithmetic just told you which problems are real: 1,200 writes/sec doesn't justify exotic machinery, while 91TB means you'll be splitting data eventually and should choose a key that doesn't fight you. This is why estimation comes first — thirty seconds of division stopped you from designing for a bottleneck you don't have.

exercises.title: A short code is something you hand out, not something you compute from the URL
exercises.body: Two families. Hash the long URL and keep 7 characters: the code is now a *function* of the input. Or keep a counter and hand out the next number, written in base62: the code is an *identity* you assign. Notice what the diagram is missing — no arrow from the URL to the counter. The counter never looks at what you're shortening.
exercises.note: Collisions are the smaller objection — a clash is detectable, so you redraw. Determinism has no redraw: the same URL always yields the same code, so two customers shortening one link must share it, analytics and all.

exercises.prompt: Your short code is 7 characters from [a-zA-Z0-9] — 62 possibilities per character. How many links can that address?
exercises.why: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion, which at 100M links/day is roughly 95 years of headroom — so 7 characters is a defensible choice you can justify with arithmetic rather than taste. That's the useful move: the length of the code is a capacity decision, and 6 characters (~57 billion) would run out in under two years at this rate.

exercises.prompt: Approach A: hash the long URL (say MD5) and take the first 7 characters. What's the problem?
choices: Truncating a hash produces collisions — two different URLs can map to the same 7 characters, so you must detect that and handle it on every write
exercises.why: Any function mapping unlimited inputs into 3.5 trillion outputs must collide eventually, and by the birthday paradox it starts happening far earlier than intuition suggests. So hashing doesn't remove the problem, it just means every insert needs a uniqueness check and a retry strategy — which is workable, and it's real complexity on the write path.

exercises.prompt: Approach B: use an auto-incrementing counter and encode the number in base62. What does that buy?
choices: No collisions ever, by construction — each number is used once, and base62 just changes how you write it down
exercises.why: Uniqueness comes free from the counter rather than being checked for, so the write path has no collision logic at all — and base62 is purely a rendering of the same integer, not a hash. Codes also stay short early on, since link one is 'b' rather than seven random characters.

exercises.prompt: What are the real downsides of the counter approach? Select all.
choices: Codes are sequential, so anyone can enumerate every link ever created
It reveals roughly how many links you've made — a business metric you may not want public
A single global counter is a coordination point that must be unique across all servers
exercises.why: Guessability is the serious one: sequential codes mean a scraper can walk your entire corpus, and 'unlisted' links stop being unlisted. It also leaks your growth rate, and the counter itself becomes something every server must agree on. What it never does is collide — that was the whole point.

exercises.prompt: So how do you get a counter without every write hitting one coordination point?
choices: Hand each server a pre-allocated range — server A gets 1–10,000, B gets 10,001–20,000 — so servers only coordinate once per block, not once per link
Let each server keep its own counter
exercises.why: Range allocation amortizes the coordination: one agreement buys ten thousand IDs, so the shared counter is touched once per block instead of 1,200 times a second. This is a genuinely reusable trick — batch the coordination rather than eliminating it — and the cost is gaps in the sequence when a server dies holding an unused block, which nobody cares about.

exercises.prompt: Your product promises that unlisted links can't be discovered by strangers. Slide toward your key scheme.
exercises.rightLabel: Random key + uniqueness check (unguessable, must retry)
exercises.why: You just promised unguessability, and a sequential code makes enumeration trivial — so the counter's elegance is disqualified by the requirement rather than by engineering. Random keys plus a unique constraint cost you a retry when you draw an occupied one: by year five you've stored ~182 billion links in a 3.5-trillion space, so about 5% of inserts collide and redraw. Cheap, but a real loop rather than a rounding error. And note why redrawing works here but not for the truncated hash: the hash of a given URL is always the same value, so a collision recurs forever unless you add a salt or counter, whereas a random key just draws again and moves on. Same collision odds, very different escape route.

exercises.title: The mapping never changes, and that one fact hands you the entire read path
exercises.body: A short code points at one long URL forever. Nothing to invalidate, nothing that drifts, no write-back — the hard half of unit 13 doesn't exist here, because immutable data can be copied anywhere and still can't be wrong. So the question stops being *how* to serve 116,000 redirects a second. It becomes what you'd give up to make them cheap.
exercises.note: Immutability was a choice, not luck: you decided a code points at one URL for life rather than letting people re-target a link later. Shorteners that sell an editable destination hand this whole chapter back.

exercises.prompt: 116,000 redirects/sec, and the same popular links are requested constantly. Add the piece that absorbs that read load.
exercises.why: Link mappings are perfect cache material: immutable once created, tiny, and massively skewed — a small number of links take most of the traffic. A cache in front of the database turns 116,000 database reads/sec into a few thousand, and the database keeps being the source of truth for everything that misses.

exercises.prompt: Why are these mappings unusually good cache candidates?
choices: They never change: a short code maps to one long URL forever, so a cached entry can't go stale — which deletes unit 5's invalidation problem entirely
exercises.why: Cache invalidation is hard because copies drift from a truth that keeps moving — and here the truth never moves, so the whole category of problem evaporates. Immutable data is the easiest thing in system design, which is worth noticing as a design lever: making data immutable, where you can, buys you caching for free.

exercises.prompt: Should the redirect return 301 (permanent) or 302 (temporary)?
choices: It's a real tradeoff: 301 lets browsers cache the redirect so subsequent clicks never reach you at all, which is great for load and destroys your click analytics
exercises.why: A 301 is the best possible caching outcome and the worst possible analytics outcome, because a browser that remembers the redirect stops telling you the click happened. So the choice is decided by the product: if click counts are the business, you take 302 and eat the traffic; if they're decoration, 301 makes most of your load disappear.

exercises.prompt: Your cache holds the hot links. A brand-new viral link is created and instantly gets 50,000 requests/second. What happens?
choices: The first requests all miss simultaneously and stampede the database for the same key — a thundering herd on one row
exercises.why: A cold key under sudden load means thousands of concurrent misses each dutifully going to the database for the identical value, which is unit 14's stampede at the row level. The fix is request coalescing: let one miss fetch while the rest wait for its result, so each server makes one query instead of thousands. Be precise about what that buys, though — coalescing is per-process, so the database sees one query per SERVER rather than one overall, and a fleet serving 116,000 rps is many servers. Getting to a single fetch needs a shared lease, or a shielding tier in front of the store — exactly the move unit 14 makes with origin shielding when 300 edges each coalesce and the origin still sees 300.

exercises.prompt: Which database fits this workload?
choices: It must be relational for the transactions
Almost anything: the access pattern is a key-value lookup by short code, so a KV store fits perfectly — and it's the access pattern, not fashion, that says so
It must be NoSQL for the scale
exercises.why: The system does exactly one read: give me the long URL for this code. That's a hashmap, which is unit 7's cleanest case — no joins, no transactions, no ad-hoc queries. Postgres would serve this happily too; what makes the KV store defensible is that the workload genuinely has one access pattern, and that's the honest reasoning rather than 'NoSQL scales'.

exercises.prompt: How would you shard 91TB of links?
choices: By hash of the short code — it's the only thing every read has, and hashing spreads the hot codes across shards
exercises.why: Unit 15's rule is to shard by what your hot query filters on, and every redirect arrives knowing exactly one thing: the short code. Sharding by date would send all of today's traffic to today's shard — the sequential-key hotspot — and sharding by user would mean the redirect, which has no user, can't find its row without a scan.

exercises.title: You only built one map, and every feature you add later lands in it
exercises.body: A custom alias like `/launch` isn't a separate feature with its own storage. It's a row in the same map as every generated code — a key somebody chose rather than drew. So two parties now write into one namespace, neither of them coordinating, and `/launch` is free only if nothing ever generated it first.
exercises.note: Your own product lives in that namespace too: `/about`, `/pricing`, `/api`. A generator that emits one of those doesn't collide with a customer — it collides with your website. That's what reserved prefixes are for.

exercises.prompt: A user wants the custom alias `/launch`. How does that interact with your generated keys?
choices: They share one namespace, so a custom alias can collide with a generated one — you need a uniqueness constraint over both, and generated keys ideally shouldn't land on nice words
Generate the custom alias by hashing it
exercises.why: Both are just keys in the same map, so `/launch` is only free if nothing generated it first — and a unique constraint in the database is the only enforcement that can't be raced (unit 6). Real systems often generate from a reduced alphabet or reserve a prefix space, so generated codes and human-chosen words rarely compete for the same string.

exercises.prompt: Links can expire. How do you delete 100 million expired links a day?
choices: A nightly DELETE query across the table
Don't delete on read paths — either let the store expire them by TTL, or sweep in small batches, because one enormous DELETE will lock and lag everything
exercises.why: A single mass DELETE is a long-running transaction touching millions of rows, which is unit 9's advice violated at scale — it holds locks, bloats storage, and lags your replicas exactly when it runs. A TTL that the store enforces, or small idempotent batches, keeps the work bounded and interruptible, which is what makes it safe to run on a live system.

exercises.prompt: You want click analytics, but writing a row per click means 116,000 writes/sec — 100× your link writes. What do you do?
choices: Fire the click onto a queue and aggregate asynchronously — the redirect must not wait for analytics, and approximate counts are fine
exercises.why: Analytics would be the single largest write load in the system, and it's the least important data — so it must never sit on the redirect's critical path (unit 16). Queue the event, batch the aggregation, and accept that a few lost clicks change no decision anyone will ever make, which is exactly the durability tradeoff unit 6 described.

exercises.prompt: Which parts of this system genuinely need strong consistency? Select all.
choices: The uniqueness of a short code
The mapping visible immediately after creation, to the creator
exercises.why: Uniqueness is non-negotiable — two long URLs behind one code is corruption you can't undo — and the creator seeing their own new link immediately is unit 19's read-your-writes, which is what they'd notice. The counter and the dashboards can be seconds or minutes stale and nobody is harmed, so paying for coordination there buys a guarantee nobody would miss.

exercises.prompt: Someone shortens a malicious URL and it spreads. What have you built without meaning to?
choices: An anonymizer: your trusted domain now launders links whose destination nobody can see before clicking
exercises.why: The product's core feature — hiding the destination behind your domain — is exactly what makes it useful for phishing, so abuse isn't a bolt-on concern but a direct consequence of the design. That's why real shorteners check destinations against blocklists, rate limit creation, and offer a preview: the mitigation belongs in the design, because the vulnerability came from the requirements.

exercises.prompt: Summarize the design in one line.
choices: A distributed database with complex sharding
A key-value lookup that's overwhelmingly read-heavy and immutable — so the design is a cache in front of a KV store, and the interesting decisions are key generation, analytics, and abuse
A microservices architecture with a message bus
A relational database with heavy indexing
exercises.why: The arithmetic said writes were easy and reads were everything, and immutability said caching is free — so the core is genuinely simple, and pretending otherwise is how people over-engineer this in interviews. All the real difficulty sits at the edges: how you mint keys, how you count clicks without drowning, and what happens when people misuse it.
